title: ExploreKarnataka.com – site overview
source_page_title: Explore Heritage – ExploreKarnataka.com
text:
ExploreKarnataka.com is a tourism website, described in its footer as a unit of DestinationMantra.com and based in Bengaluru. Its main menu offers Home, Explore Heritage, Explore Divinity, Explore Cities, Blog, About Us and Contact.

The Explore Heritage index says Karnataka has many historic and heritage monuments and that the site keeps adding monuments, towns and cities. It lists six heritage entries: Aihole (cradle of Indian temple architecture), Hampi (capital of the Vijayanagara Empire), Somanathapura (Hoysala architecture, Keshava Temple), Sandur (temple complex of Parvathi and Kumaraswamy on Kraunjagiri Hill), Belur (the hallmark of Hoysala heritage) and Mirjan Fort (the Pepper Queen's fortress).

The index blurb for Belur says the Hoysalas ruled southern India between the 11th and 14th centuries, that they mastered the temple art after the Chalukyas experimented with it, and that more than 1000 temples were built in their period.

[AI note] Only the Belur entry is in scope for this knowledge base. The other five entries were discovered but not processed (see manifest).

qa_pairs.question: Which heritage places does ExploreKarnataka list on its heritage index?
qa_pairs.answer: Aihole, Hampi, Somanathapura, Sandur, Belur and Mirjan Fort.

title: Historical background (ExploreKarnataka)
source_page_title: Belur – The Hallmark of Hoysala Heritage – ExploreKarnataka.com
source_heading: Beluru – The Hallmark of Hoysala Heritage / Channakeshava Temple
text:
Beluru, also written Belur, is a small town in Hassan district, Karnataka, known for temples and monuments that show Hoysala artistic and architectural skill. It was once the Hoysala capital and was then called Velapuri. The page says the Hoysalas ruled most of South India from the 10th to the 14th century from two capitals at different times: Beluru (Velapuri) and Halebeedu (Dwarasamudra).

According to the page, King Vishnuvardhana built the Chennakeshava Temple in 1117 CE to mark his victory over the Cholas, and completing it took more than a century. The old capital Velapuri was founded on the banks of the Yagachi River.

The Sowmyanayaki temple is described as Hoysala-period and renovated under Vijayanagara rule in 1387. The Ranganayaki (Andal) temple is said, per an ASI plaque outside it, to have been built by the Vijayanagara kings from material of ruined nearby Hoysala-period temples.

qa_pairs.question: What was Belur called in Hoysala times?
qa_pairs.answer: Velapuri (ExploreKarnataka).

qa_pairs.question: Who built the Chennakeshava Temple and when?
qa_pairs.answer: King Vishnuvardhana, in 1117 CE, to mark his victory over the Cholas, according to ExploreKarnataka.

qa_pairs.question: What were the two Hoysala capitals?
qa_pairs.answer: Beluru (Velapuri) and Halebeedu (Dwarasamudra).

qa_pairs.question: How long did the temple take to build?
qa_pairs.answer: ExploreKarnataka says more than a century; Temples.bio says 103 years.

title: Historical background (Temples.bio)
source_page_title: Chennakeshava Temple Belur – Hoysala Carvings, Timings & Guide | Temples.bio
text:
Temples.bio says the temple took 103 years to build and calls it a 12th-century UNESCO World Heritage Site of 'National Significance'. Its architecture entry gives the style as Hoysala Architecture (Early Period) and the date 1117 CE (Hoysala dynasty).

The About text says the sculptors of Belur and Halebidu in the 12th century were effectively writing encyclopaedias in stone: every surface of the Chennakeshava Temple (Belur) and the Hoysaleswara Temple (Halebidu) carries figures of mythology, daily life, armies, elephants and love poetry. The page recommends spending a full day because not everything can be seen.

Temples.bio states the temple's rituals have been maintained for 900 years by the same hereditary priest families.

qa_pairs.question: How old is the Chennakeshava Temple?
qa_pairs.answer: Begun in 1117 CE (both sources) and described as about 900 years old in ritual continuity by Temples.bio.

title: Architecture, sculpture and carved details (ExploreKarnataka)
source_page_title: Belur – The Hallmark of Hoysala Heritage – ExploreKarnataka.com
text:
The Chennakeshava Temple (also Keshava Temple or Belur Temple) is dedicated to Vishnu and is called one of the finest examples of Hoysala architecture. It is decorated with fine soapstone carvings showing scenes from the Hindu epics and Puranas. The page also mentions a 100-feet high tower, a grand entrance gate and a six-feet tall Vishnu idol in the sanctum.

The author remarks that it is hard to believe such fine filigree could be made in stone and that the skill of the Hoysala artisans is beyond words.

Photographs on the page document: the main entrance, whose door jamb shows Ugra Narasimha mounted on Garuda slaying the demon Hiranyakashyapa (IMG-0002); the Hoysala emblem, a warrior hunting a lion (IMG-0003, IMG-0004); an interior array of high-precision circular pillars (IMG-0006); carved dwara palakas (door guardians) at the inner sanctum (IMG-0007, IMG-0016); stone-carved maidens, one holding a staff with a skull and wearing a skull-decorated crown (IMG-0008, IMG-0009) and others playing drums and dancing (IMG-0010 to IMG-0013); and Ugra Narasimha slaying Hiranyakashyapa and garlanding the intestines, seen both on the outer wall and on an interior ceiling (IMG-0014, IMG-0015).

[AI note] The image filenames use the word 'shilabalike' for the maiden carvings and 'jaya-vijaya' for the door guardians. The source captions do not use those words, so they are filename evidence only. No image was visually inspected for this document; descriptions are limited to the source captions.

[AI note] IMG-0017 (exterior view) has no caption on the source page and its subject is unverified.

qa_pairs.answer: Soapstone, per both ExploreKarnataka and Temples.bio (Temples.bio specifies black soapstone).

title: Architecture, sculpture and carved details (Temples.bio)
source_page_title: Chennakeshava Temple Belur – Hoysala Carvings, Timings & Guide | Temples.bio
source_heading: Architecture & Heritage / Spiritual Highlights / Rituals & Traditions
text:
Temples.bio describes the temple as standing on a star-shaped platform in black soapstone, with every inch carved. Architecture highlights listed: the 42 Madanika bracket figures, the rotating pillar, and the monolithic lotus ceiling of the Navaranga. The 42 Madanika figures are called the finest stone figurative carvings in South Asia.

Sacred objects listed: the Darpana Sundari (Lady with Mirror) carving on the outer wall and the queen Shanthala's Garuda pillar inscription. Devotee practices include walking around the platform to observe more than 10,000 carvings and hiring a guide to read the Puranic narratives.

Special tradition listed: a 'gravity-defying pillar in the courtyard' under which a sheet of paper can be passed because it rests on its own centre of mass.

[AI note] Unclear whether the 'rotating pillar' and the 'gravity-defying pillar' are the same object; the page does not say. Not resolved here.

qa_pairs.question: How many Madanika figures does Temples.bio mention?
qa_pairs.answer: 42 Madanika bracket figures.

qa_pairs.question: What is the Darpana Sundari?
qa_pairs.answer: A carving called the 'Lady with Mirror' on the outer wall, which Temples.bio says is believed to bring beauty and grace to those who observe it sincerely.

qa_pairs.question: What inscription is mentioned?
qa_pairs.answer: Queen Shanthala's Garuda pillar inscription (Temples.bio lists it as a sacred object; no text of the inscription is given).

title: Kappe Chennigaraya Temple
source_page_title: Belur – The Hallmark of Hoysala Heritage – ExploreKarnataka.com
text:
A smaller temple inside the same compound, adjacent to the main temple. Local lore holds that the deity here was carved to be the main statue to be worshipped inside the Keshava Temple, and the page says there is an interesting tale of how it came to be worshipped at the nearby smaller shrine. The page does not retell that tale.

[AI note] The tale is not given in the source and is not supplied here.

title: Sowmyanayaki Temple
source_page_title: Belur – The Hallmark of Hoysala Heritage – ExploreKarnataka.com
text: Dedicated to Goddess Lakshmi, consort of Vishnu. It lies to the south-west of the Keshava Temple within the same complex. Historians think it was built in the Hoysala period and renovated under the Vijayanagara kings in 1387.

qa_pairs.question: Where is the Sowmyanayaki temple?
qa_pairs.answer: South-west of the Keshava Temple, inside the same complex.

title: Ranganayaki (Andal Amma) Temple
source_page_title: Belur – The Hallmark of Hoysala Heritage – ExploreKarnataka.com
text:
Dedicated to Andal Amma, believed to be an incarnation of Bhudevi, consort of Vishnu, according to Alvar traditions. It stands at the north-western end of the complex. An ASI plaque outside says the Vijayanagara kings built it using material from ruined Hoysala-period temples nearby.

IMG-0005 caption: Ranganayaki Temple or Andal Temple within the premises of Chennakeshava Temple, Belur.

qa_pairs.question: Who built the Andal temple?
qa_pairs.answer: The Vijayanagara kings, per an ASI plaque cited by ExploreKarnataka, reusing material from ruined Hoysala-era temples.

image_descriptions.IMG-0005: Source caption: Ranganayaki Temple or Andal Temple within the premises of Chennakeshava Temple, Belur.

title: Sri Pathaleshwara Temple
source_page_title: Belur – The Hallmark of Hoysala Heritage – ExploreKarnataka.com
text: About half a kilometre from the Chennakeshava Temple. A smaller Shiva temple with an intricately carved thorana (ornamental archway); the page says it lacks the grandeur of other Hoysala temples.

title: Yagachi Dam
source_page_title: Belur – The Hallmark of Hoysala Heritage – ExploreKarnataka.com
text: Built on the Yagachi River, about 3 km from the Chennakeshava Temple. The backwater offers water sports including kayaking and banana boat rides. The page advises checking holidays and seasonality with the operators.

title: Deity, rituals and religious practice
source_page_title: Chennakeshava Temple Belur – Hoysala Carvings, Timings & Guide | Temples.bio
text:
Primary deity is Chennakeshava (Vishnu). Temples.bio says daily rituals have been maintained for 900 years by the same hereditary priest families. Spiritual benefits listed: artistic inspiration, appreciation of devotional perfection and spiritual focus through aesthetic concentration.

Prasada available: laddu and pongal (pongal on festival days). A laddu is listed at Rs. 30 on the timings page.

title: Festivals and events
source_page_title: Chennakeshava Temple Belur – Hoysala Carvings, Timings & Guide | Temples.bio
text:
Major festivals: Hoysala Mahotsava, Annual Rathotsava and Vaikunta Ekadashi. Special events: classical Bharatanatyam and Yakshagana performances in the Navaranga Mandapa during heritage festivals.

The timings page lists Belur Rathotsava in April: a massive wooden chariot pulled through Belur town by thousands of devotees, with a very high crowd level. Dates change each year with the Hindu calendar and should be verified before planning (https://www.temples.bio/temples/chennakeshava-temple-belur/timings).

Temples.bio recommends winter mornings (October–February) for clear light on the black soapstone and manageable crowds.

qa_pairs.question: When is the Belur Rathotsava?
qa_pairs.answer: Listed for April; the exact date varies by Hindu calendar (Temples.bio).

qa_pairs.question: Which festivals does Temples.bio list for the temple?
qa_pairs.answer: Hoysala Mahotsava, Annual Rathotsava and Vaikunta Ekadashi.

title: Location and how to reach
source_page_title: Belur – The Hallmark of Hoysala Heritage – ExploreKarnataka.com
source_heading: Travel to Belur / Photos; Temples.bio How to Reach
text:
Map coordinates embedded on Temples.bio: 13.163354043883, 75.860899613494 (from the embedded Google Maps URL).

ExploreKarnataka: best time October to March. By road, Belur is linked to Bengaluru, Mysore, Mangalore, Madikeri, Shimoga, Chikmagalur and Hassan by private and state buses, about 220 km from Bengaluru mostly via NH 75. Hassan, the district headquarters, is about 38 km away with state buses roughly every half hour.

By train, the nearest station is Hassan (about 38 km), connected to Bengaluru, Mysore, Mangalore, Hubli, Dharwad and Karwar. By air, the nearest airport is Bengaluru (BLR), about 220 km; the page says Hassan has an airport under construction that was not operational when the page was written.

Temples.bio: nearest airport Kempegowda International, Bengaluru (220 km, about 3.5 hours by road); nearest railway Hassan (38 km, about 50 minutes); nearest bus stop Belur Bus Stand (500 m walk). Tip: hire a government-approved guide at the entrance and combine with Halebidu (16 km) in the same day.

qa_pairs.question: What is the nearest railway station to Belur?
qa_pairs.answer: Hassan, about 38 km away.

qa_pairs.question: How far is Belur from Bengaluru?
qa_pairs.answer: About 220 km by road, mostly on NH 75, per ExploreKarnataka; 220 km to the airport, about 3.5 hours, per Temples.bio.

qa_pairs.question: How far is the bus stand from the temple?
qa_pairs.answer: 500 m on foot (Temples.bio).

title: Nearby Hoysala heritage towns and temples
source_page_title: Belur – The Hallmark of Hoysala Heritage – ExploreKarnataka.com
text:
Hassan city has several temples and attractions. Other Hoysala temple towns near Beluru: Halebeedu (17 km), Doddagaddavalli Laxmi Temple (24 km, on the Hassan–Belur highway), Belavadi Veera Narayana Swamy Temple (28 km from Belur, 12 km from Halebeedu) and Javagal Narasimha Temple (28 km from Belur, 12 km from Halebeedu, 8.7 km from Belavadi).

qa_pairs.question: What other Hoysala temples are near Belur?
qa_pairs.answer: Halebeedu (17 km), Doddagaddavalli (24 km), Belavadi (28 km) and Javagal (28 km), per ExploreKarnataka.

title: Temples near Belur (Temples.bio city guide)
source_page_title: Temples in Belur: Map, Route & 1–2 Day Darshan Guide
text:
Temples.bio's city guide lists 19 temples 'in and around Belur', ordered by pilgrimage importance and driving distance from Belur. The table gives the distance in km from the city guide cards; in brackets is the distance shown on the temple profile page (https://www.temples.bio/temples/chennakeshava-temple-belur) where that page lists the temple and the figure differs or is given.

Guide advice: October to March is most comfortable; summer afternoons are tiring, so plan early darshan. The main temples of Belur can be covered in about 2 days; most visitors can do 4 to 6 temples in a day if they start early and stay local. For families and seniors a hired cab or auto-rickshaw is simpler.

The guide also gives a 9-day route: Day 1 Chennakeshava; Day 2 Sakleshwara; Day 3 Kukke Subramanya and Dharmasthala; Day 4 Gommateshwara, Hornadu and Sringeri Mahalakshmi; Day 5 Sringeri Sharada Peetham, Bhoo Varaha, Melkote; Day 6 Bhoga Nandishwara, Kateel, Nimishambha; Day 7 Srirangapatna Ranganathaswamy, Chamundeshwari, Chitradurga; Day 8 Udupi and Madhur; Day 9 Shivagange.

title: Visitor guidelines, facilities and accessibility
source_page_title: Chennakeshava Temple Belur – Hoysala Carvings, Timings & Guide | Temples.bio
source_heading: Visitor Guidelines / Practical Information / How to Reach
text:
Dress code: modest clothing; footwear removed on the temple platform. Accessibility: described as good, with a flat elevated platform and wide walkways around the perimeter. Parking: available. Entry fee: free.

Temples.bio travel tips: visit October–March for cool weather and the best light on the carvings; hire a government-approved guide at the entrance because the stories of the 42 Madanikas alone are worth an hour; combine with Halebidu the same day.

Accommodation: ExploreKarnataka says Belur has a few lodges, including the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation's Mayura Velapuri, and that more luxurious stays are in Hassan. Temples.bio shows an accommodation promotion near the temple 'starting from Rs. 950' (promotional banner; no property named).

[AI note] No official ASI or temple-authority rules (photography, bag storage, shoe stand locations) appear on the pages crawled.

qa_pairs.question: Is there a dress code?
qa_pairs.answer: Modest clothing is advised and footwear must be removed on the temple platform (Temples.bio).

qa_pairs.question: Is the temple wheelchair accessible?
qa_pairs.answer: Temples.bio calls accessibility good, with a flat raised platform and wide walkways; no detail on ramps or steps is given.

qa_pairs.question: Where can I stay in Belur?
qa_pairs.answer: A few lodges including Mayura Velapuri (KSTDC); better options in Hassan (ExploreKarnataka).

title: Conflict/uncertainty: Afternoon closure
text: Claim: Temples.bio timings page: midday/afternoon row marked 'Closed' between 1:30 PM and 4:00 PM, but the page note and the city guide say 'ASI protected monument; no afternoon closure.' Handling: Unresolved inside one source. Seen as search-result snippets only (not crawled, so not verified): other sites give 7:30 AM–7:30 PM continuous, 6 AM–8 PM, 9 AM–6 PM, and a 1:00–1:30 PM break. Confirm locally.

title: Conflict/uncertainty: Construction duration
